The production of synthetic crystals was pioneered in the late 19th century, with the first synthetic rubies produced by E. Fremy in 1877.
Over 95% of high-quality (semiconductor grade) silicon single crystals and about 45% of lower-quality (solar grade) crystals are produced by the Czochralski method.
Bulk GaN, AlN, and AlGaN crystals remain difficult to grow, with no bulk InN crystals produced to date due to the thermal instability of III-nitrides.
Ammonothermal and alkali metal flux methods have been developed to grow III-nitride crystals at lower temperatures and pressures compared to high-nitrogen pressure solution growth.
Sapphire and SiC are the best available substrates for III-nitride epitaxial growth, but still have significant lattice and thermal expansion mismatches.
The Czochralski growth of silicon crystals with diameters above 40 mm exhibits turbulent melt flow, which is challenging to model accurately using traditional RANS turbulence models.
Direct numerical simulation (DNS) of the Czochralski process is computationally prohibitive for industrial-scale crystals due to the large Reynolds numbers involved.
The high Schmidt number (Sc ≈ 10) for oxygen in molten silicon requires very fine computational grids to accurately resolve the oxygen transport.

Modeling of crystal growth processes requires the coupled solution of heat transfer by conduction, convection, and radiation, as well as mass transfer, electromagnetic effects, and crystal quality assessment.
Verification of crystal growth models is essential and involves both code verification (correct implementation) and model validation (agreement with experimental data).
Crystal growth modeling is used not only for fundamental research, but also for real-time process control and optimization of growth conditions and equipment design.
The scale-up of crystal growth equipment is challenging due to the nonlinear nature of the underlying heat and mass transfer processes.
Solvothermal methods like the ammonothermal process can compensate for the low growth rates by simultaneously growing multiple crystals (over 100 for ZnO, over 2000 for quartz).
Sublimation growth is used for SiC and AlN crystals, but is less successful for GaN due to the much higher equilibrium nitrogen pressure over the GaN surface.
Modeling of crystal growth processes often involves a global (furnace-scale) and a local (hot zone) problem, with the solutions coupled through boundary conditions.
